1:
Who the strangers set to the work were is the disagreement that matters, since it decides whether the temple was built by volunteers or by conscripts. Ellicott reads them as resident foreigners, the Canaanite population who lived on sufferance under Israelite dominion and were liable to forced service if the government required it; Solomon afterwards found them by census to be a hundred and fifty-three thousand six hundred souls, the count being a preliminary to apportioning their tasks, and what originated with David was the organisation of the serf labour rather than the building itself. Clarke takes them instead for men who had become proselytes, at least so far as to renounce idolatry and keep the seven Noahic precepts, and says they were employed in the more servile and difficult parts of the work. Gill agrees that they were proselytes of the gate who had submitted to the precepts of Noah, and gives two reasons for using them: partly that they were better artificers than the Israelites, who were chiefly employed in husbandry and cattle, and partly that the Israelites, being freemen, might not be put to hard service.

How young Solomon was is unsettled, and Ellicott shows why the word cannot settle it. The term rendered young is even vaguer than the Latin adolescens, since it may mean a new-born babe, a young child, a youth, or a man in the prime of life, and it is applied to Rehoboam at forty-one; Solomon calls himself a young child after his accession. Ellicott would also render the companion word timid rather than tender. Gill reports Jarchi's supposition of twelve while noting that the same word is used of Joshua at forty-two, and concludes Solomon was probably about twenty. Henry does not date him but draws the motive from the description: Solomon being young and tender was not likely to apply with great vigour at first, and unless he found the wheels already turning would lose time, whereas with the materials ready to his hand the most difficult part would be over and he would be encouraged to begin early in his reign. Those who are aged and experienced, Henry adds, should provide what help they can for those who are young, to make the work of God as easy to them as possible.

On the quantities Ellicott is cool where the others are not. He calls the iron and brass without weight a natural hyperbole and the cedars without number a rhetorical exaggeration, since the actual amounts would of course be known to the royal treasurers, and compares the Assyrian habit of reckoning spoils without number or measure. He adds that bronze was much used in the ornamental work of ancient buildings, and explains the cedar as ordinary commerce, the Phoenicians bartering timber for grain and wine and oil their own rocky coast did not yield. Delitzsch adds that the Sidonians and Tyrians are named to denote the Phoenicians generally. Henry reads the site rather than the materials: the ground chosen pertained to a Jebusite, which he takes for a happy presage of the gospel temple set up among the Gentiles, and it was a threshing-floor, the church of the living God being his floor and his threshing. This is the house, Henry says, because this is the altar: the temple was built for the sake of the altar, and there were altars long before temples. Clarke puts it practically: until a temple was built this place was to be considered the temple of God, and on this altar and not the one at Gibeon the burnt offerings of Israel were to be made. Ellicott sees further, that the whole narrative of the census and the pestilence has its goal here, and that the chronicler would probably have omitted it, as he omitted the famine, but that it shows how the temple site was determined.
6:
Ellicott opens the charge with the most radical claim in the chapter. On grounds of internal evidence, he says, we may pronounce this dying address an ideal composition, put into the king's mouth by the unknown author whose work the chronicler follows, or rather perhaps by the chronicler himself, whose style is evident throughout; and he compares the addresses attributed to David later in the book and the echoes he hears of the dying charge in Kings. He fixes the occasion shortly before David's death, and notes that the Hebrew reads his son where the margin and the versions rightly give my son, probably an oversight carried from the preceding verse.

Why David was barred draws three accounts from the sources Ellicott sets side by side. Here the reason is blood, which Ellicott would render literally as torrents of blood shed earthward; he thinks the author may well have remembered the charge against the shedder of man's blood in Genesis and the prophets' denunciations of men of blood. But he points out that the oracle Nathan delivered promises success in war without any hint that warfare as such would unfit David for the sacred task, and that in Kings Solomon implies rather that his father's wars left him no leisure. Henry meets the difficulty from the other side, dismissing the suggestion that the blood meant is Uriah's, since the honour was forbidden before that blood was shed, and concluding it must be the blood of his wars, which though shed justly and honourably still made him less fit for this service than one never called to such work. From that Henry draws two inferences: that God showed how precious human life is to him, and that he intended a type of the builder of the gospel temple, who should build not by destroying men's lives but by saving them. Clarke generalises furthest, observing that heathens, Jews and Christians have all agreed that soldiers of any kind should have nothing to do with divine offices, the shedding of human blood ill comporting with the benevolence of God; and he illustrates it from the flight out of Troy, where the hero, just come from slaughter, would not handle the household gods himself but confided them to his father, holding it impious to touch holy things while red with new blood until he had washed in some living stream.

On the promise and the charge they converge. Ellicott renders the key phrases as wishes rather than commands, so that they mean may you prosper and build, and at least may the Lord give you wisdom, the restriction marking one supremely important point; and he notes that the blessing is the origin of the familiar liturgical formula. He insists that the verse about prospering makes clear that obedience was an indispensable condition of the promise being fully realised, and adds that although the earthly dynasty ended through disobedience the word of the Lord did not return void, since in due time an heir of David and Solomon was born whose spiritual dominion endures. He also defends the prayer against the charge of superfluity: Solomon was already indicated as successor and David intended it so, yet the wish for divine ratification was not idle unless Solomon were exempt from liability to err. Henry reads the appointment as the ground of courage, since nothing is more powerful to engage us in any service for God than to know that hereunto we are appointed, and takes the promised rest as the opportunity rather than the reward, Solomon being a man of rest who would not have his time or thoughts or wealth diverted; where God gives rest, Henry says, he expects work. Gill reports the Targum turning the blessing into a prayer that the Word of the Lord may be his help.
17:
The charge to the princes is read chiefly as a point about how work gets done. Henry puts it plainly: those who are in the throne cannot do the good they would unless those about the throne set in with them, and David therefore wanted the princes to advise Solomon and quicken him and make the work as easy to him as they could, each promoting it in his own place. He finds their obligation in gratitude, since God had given them victory and rest and a good land for an inheritance, and the more God has done for us the more we should study to do for him. On the appeal to the heart he is most insistent: they are to place their happiness in God's favour and keep their eye on his glory, seeking him as their chief good and highest end, and then they will grudge no pains nor cost to promote the building of his sanctuary; let the heart be sincerely engaged and the head and hand, the estate and interest, and all will be cheerfully employed. He closes with an encouragement for those who see little result, that much good may appear after our death which we never thought of, so that we should not be weary of well doing, the work being in the hands of the Prince of peace.

Ellicott makes the same connection grammatically rather than devotionally. He would render the command as arise ye and build, holding that the second clause explains how the first was to be carried out, so that building the Lord a fair and noble sanctuary was equivalent to seeking his favour; professions cost nothing, he adds, and they were not to serve the Lord without cost. He notes that the phrase here is to seek unto the Lord, the later construction, where the older books use a simple accusative, and that the word saying is absent from the Hebrew text, as it is at several other places in this book. On the preceding question he would drop the interrogative in the second clause and read it as a statement, that he has given you rest, and he takes the inhabitants given into David's hand to be the surrounding peoples whose reduction the earlier chapters describe, the chronicler or his authority thinking of the language of Numbers and Joshua about a land subdued before the Lord. The ark, he observes, was to come from its temporary abode on Mount Zion.

Clarke supplies the political reckoning and then turns it into a lament. David at this time was not only king of Judea but had subdued most of the surrounding nations, so that Solomon came to the Jewish throne with every possible advantage; and had he made a proper use of his state and of his talents he would have been the greatest as well as the wisest of sovereigns. But alas, Clarke says, how soon did this pure gold become dim. He traces the decline in order, beginning with an unlawful matrimonial connection, which led to a commerce positively forbidden by the law of God, and then to the multiplying of connections with heathen women who turned his heart away. Clarke also quotes the Targum again for the opening question, which it turns into an assurance that the Word of the Lord is their assistant. Gill reads the same question as a reference to the wealth and riches with which God had blessed them, and takes the charge to seek God as meaning his honour and glory, sought most sincerely and cordially and to the utmost of their power.
